title: Job interviews and whether they predict anything

turns.speaker: Ross
turns.text: Seven interviews for one role. Seven. And the last one was a chat about whether he'd fit the team.

turns.speaker: Aya
turns.text: Which is the stage with the worst predictive record of anything they did.

turns.speaker: Dermot
turns.text: How bad is unstructured interviewing, actually? I've heard it's poor but not the number.

turns.speaker: Aya
turns.text: It correlates with later performance at somewhere around point two. A work sample test is roughly double that.

turns.speaker: Ross
turns.text: So the cheapest and most popular method is the least useful.

turns.speaker: Aya
turns.text: And the confidence people have in their own judgement is completely uncorrelated with their accuracy, which is the genuinely uncomfortable finding.

turns.speaker: Dermot
turns.text: Fit is the part I'd challenge hardest. It usually means somebody the panel would enjoy having lunch with.

turns.speaker: Ross
turns.text: Which reliably produces a team of the same kind of person.

turns.speaker: Aya
turns.text: Structured interviews do much better. Same questions, same order, scored against agreed criteria, and interviewers who don't confer first.

turns.speaker: Dermot
turns.text: Nobody likes doing them, though. They feel robotic.

turns.speaker: Aya
turns.text: They feel worse and work better, which is true of most debiasing.

turns.speaker: Ross
turns.text: The seven rounds are their own problem regardless. The good candidates take another offer by round four.

turns.speaker: Dermot
turns.text: So a long process selects for whoever had no alternatives.

points: A hiring process used seven interviews, ending with an unstructured discussion about team fit.
Unstructured interviews correlate with later performance at around 0.2, roughly half the predictive value of work sample tests.
Interviewer confidence is uncorrelated with accuracy.
Dermot argues fit usually means social similarity, producing homogeneous teams.
Structured interviews with identical questions, agreed criteria and independent scoring perform substantially better despite feeling mechanical.
Ross notes long processes lose strong candidates to other offers, so they select for those without alternatives.
